title: DNA between 622 CRISPRi-validated human enhancers and their target genes changed length 9-15% less than matched control DNA in 11 non-primate mammals, with no dosage dependence
abstract: Across mammals, the DNA between a human enhancer and the gene that it controls changed in length only slightly less than matched control DNA, and this small difference did not depend on how sensitive the gene is to its dose. This matters because a function that depends on the total length of DNA, and not on its sequence, would add functional DNA that sequence- and indel-based conservation estimates do not count. We used 622 enhancer-gene pairs that CRISPR interference (CRISPRi: silencing of an element in its native place) showed to be functional, mostly in K562 cells, and 10,097 tested pairs without an effect. For each pair we measured the human interval from enhancer to promoter (the link) and two same-length flanks, and read their lengths in 15 mammals from UCSC chain alignments. Typical intervals changed length by 18% in 11 non-primate placentals and by 2.6% in 3 primates. We compared the link-minus-flank change of validated pairs with that of negative pairs of the same geometry (difference in differences), with adjustment for conserved, exonic and gene-body DNA. In non-primates the link changed 0.855 times as much as expected (95% CI 0.715-0.993, p = 0.039); without adjustment 0.91 (0.77-1.05). Against the outer flank alone the ratio was 0.86 (p = 0.006), against the opposite flank 0.93 (p = 0.54). All 14 placental species gave ratios of 0.70-0.93; primates gave 0.75 (0.54-0.97). So a reduction of about 9-15% is likely, and more than about 30% is excluded. A stabilizing-selection model, in which an enhancer's contribution falls with distance to the power alpha and fitness falls with the square of the expression change scaled by s_het (the fitness cost of losing one gene copy), predicted a ratio of 0.52 for non-primates (population size 10^4, alpha = 0.87 as in contact-based enhancer models) and a steep gradient with s_het. The data need the model's selection strength to be at least 5 times weaker, and the observed gradient was -0.012 +/- 0.014 per 10-fold s_het against a predicted -0.06 to -0.09. Synteny of the link did not differ from controls. Two independent reviews changed the primary analysis; the pre-specified test gave 0.90 (0.77-1.03). Limits: the enhancers may not be active in other mammals; the flanks are imperfect controls; the significance depends on covariate adjustment. A cross-species CRISPRi experiment can tell whether expression or fitness is insensitive to these distance changes.

display.caption: A: design. Each CRISPRi-tested enhancer-gene pair gives three human intervals of the same length: enhancer to TSS (link), an outer flank and an opposite flank. B: length change of the link relative to controls for validated pairs (ratio with 95% CI) in eight analysis variants, for 11 non-primate placentals and 3 primates, with the prediction of the stabilizing-selection model (orange). The diamond is the revised primary analysis (geometry-matched difference in differences against negative pairs).

Observed covariate-adjusted matched difference-in-differences ratio (blue line, 95% CI band) against the predictions of a stabilizing-selection model (orange) with effective population size N and distance elasticity alpha, for primates and non-primate placentals; right: observed gradient of the adjusted matched difference in differences with s_het against the model gradient on the same scale.

Left: adjusted (filled, 95% CI) and unadjusted (open) matched difference-in-differences ratio (link vs both flanks) in each of 15 species. Right: raw cumulative distributions of the absolute log2 length change of validated pairs in 11 non-primate placentals; the outer flank changed more and the opposite flank less than the link.
